digest.top_line: DASL-HiCaP: darolutamide added to 96-wk ADT plus prostate/bed and pelvic nodal RT, 4-yr MFS-CI 95% vs 88%, HR 0.42 (0.27-0.66) at interim in very high-risk disease.
digest.tldr: DASL-HiCaP adds a second ARSI-intensification signal on an RT backbone: 4y MFS-CI 95% vs 88%, HR 0.42 (0.27-0.66), though at interim with OS (HR 0.88) and PCSS immature.

sites.intro: ARSI intensification on top of ADT plus pelvic nodal RT, definitive or salvage, in very high-risk disease.

studies.name: DASL-HiCaP
studies.tldr: 4-yr MFS-CI 95% vs 88%, HR 0.42 (0.27-0.66), adding darolutamide to 96-wk ADT plus prostate/bed and pelvic nodal RT in very high-risk disease.
details: 🔍 Phase III, placebo-controlled, randomised 1:1, N=1,106, international (ANZUP1801)
💊 Darolutamide 600 mg BID vs placebo for 96 wk, both arms on LHRH analog for 96 wk
🔍 RT in both arms: prostate or prostate bed plus pelvic nodes, definitive or salvage

details.text: ⚠️ Grade ≥2 AE clusters of special interest and any grade ≥3 AE

details: 📐 Single prespecified interim after 87 MFS-CI events; disclosure threshold 2-sided stratified log-rank p<0.012
📊 MFS benefit consistent across primary vs salvage RT and pelvic N+ vs N0 (OncLive); subgroup HRs not reported in source
⚠️ MFS-CI is a surrogate per ICECaP; PCSS and OS differences not established at interim
⚠️ Metastases defined on CT and/or Tc bone scan, not PSMA PET
⚠️ Prior RP in only 15%: salvage-setting estimate rests on a small subset
🔗 Same ARSI-intensification-with-RT question as ENZARAD (enzalutamide) and ATLAS (apalutamide); STAMPEDE abiraterone data frame the current high-risk bar

verdict.rationale: Prespecified interim analysis, not the final primary analysis; MFS-CI surrogate with PCSS and OS immature (OS HR 0.88, CI crosses 1). Randomised, placebo-controlled design is otherwise clean.
verdict.audience: Very high-risk localised PCa, or PSA persistent/recurrent within 1 yr of RP

studies.significance: Every pt received pelvic nodal RT with 96 wk of LHRH analog, so darolutamide's MFS-CI HR 0.42 is measured on top of elective nodal coverage, not instead of it. 29% were node-positive on CT and the benefit held across primary vs salvage RT and N+ vs N0 (subgroup HRs not in source). The decision it moves is ARSI intensification alongside whole-pelvis RT, not RT field or dose.
studies.monday_clinic: In very high-risk localised prostate cancer planned for 96 wk of ADT with prostate and pelvic nodal RT, this supports darolutamide intensification for MFS-CI; it does not yet establish an OS gain and gives thin data for post-RP salvage pts (15% of the cohort).

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: International, **placebo-controlled, randomised 1:1 phase III**, N=1,106 accrued 30APR20 to 09AUG23. **Single prespecified interim** after 87 MFS-CI events, disclosed only if 2-sided p<0.012. Median follow-up 3.8 yr (IQR 3.3-4.5).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Very high-risk localised** prostate cancer, or **biochemically persistent/recurrent disease within 1 yr after RP**. Median age 71, Gleason 9-10 in 73%, pelvic nodal involvement on CT in 29%, prior RP in 15%.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **Darolutamide 600 mg BID vs placebo for 96 wk**, both arms on an LHRH analog for 96 wk.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Definitive or salvage RT to **prostate or prostate bed plus pelvic nodes** in both arms. Dose and fractionation not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: MFS on conventional imaging (CT and/or Tc bone scan)**, chosen per ICECaP surrogacy for OS. Secondary: PSA-PFS, PCSS, OS.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary met at interim (table above). OncLive reports MFS benefit **consistent across primary vs salvage RT and N+ vs N0**, and castration resistance and subsequent hormonal therapy endpoints favouring darolutamide; no numbers given for those.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Any G≥3 AE **43% vs 36%**. G≥2 fatigue/asthenia 14% vs 10%; hypertension, fractures and cardiac events not higher with darolutamide.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Tests the same ARSI-added-to-ADT-plus-RT question as **ENZARAD** (enzalutamide) and **ATLAS** (apalutamide), and sits against the **STAMPEDE** abiraterone data that currently anchor intensification in high-risk nonmetastatic disease. DASL-HiCaP differs by mandating pelvic nodal RT and including early post-RP salvage pts.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents very high-risk localised or early post-RP persistent/recurrent prostate cancer treated with 96 wk ADT and pelvic nodal RT. Does not represent pts staged only by PSMA PET, intermediate-risk disease, or later salvage beyond 1 yr after RP.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Staging and progression on **conventional imaging** in a PSMA-era practice; salvage pts are only 15%. Backbone was **96 wk ADT plus pelvic RT** in everyone, so benefit with shorter ADT or prostate-only fields is untested.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The MFS-CI gain is large but OS events are few (21 vs 24) and PCSS is 99% in both arms at 4 yr. Whether this becomes a darolutamide option alongside abiraterone in this setting depends on surrogacy holding at final analysis.

studies.interpretation:
The question DASL-HiCaP answers is narrower than the headline suggests, and that is its strength. Radiotherapy was not randomised: every patient received prostate or prostate-bed irradiation with elective pelvic nodal coverage and 96 weeks of LHRH analog. What was tested is whether a second-generation AR inhibitor adds to an already intensive, field-generous local-plus-hormonal backbone. A metastasis-free survival hazard ratio of 0.42, with 27 versus 63 events, says it does, at least on conventional imaging. For a radiation oncologist the useful corollary is that the benefit sits on top of elective nodal RT; it gives no licence to shrink the field and no information about dose, which the source does not report.

The trial joins ENZARAD and ATLAS in asking the ARSI-plus-RT question, and it will be read against the STAMPEDE abiraterone data that currently justify intensification in high-risk nonmetastatic disease. Two design features distinguish it. Pelvic nodal RT was mandatory rather than optional, which removes one source of heterogeneity that complicates cross-trial reading. And it admitted pts with biochemically persistent or recurrent disease within a year of prostatectomy, a population that most intensification trials leave out. That inclusion is less informative than it looks: only 15% had prior RP, so the salvage estimate is drawn from a small subset, and the reported subgroup consistency comes without subgroup hazard ratios in the source.

The confidence a reader places in the result should move in two directions. Upward, because it is placebo-controlled, the interim was prespecified with a stringent disclosure threshold, and the PSA-PFS signal (HR 0.47) runs in the same direction. Downward, because this is an interim read of a surrogate. The authors chose MFS-CI on the strength of ICECaP surrogacy, but that validation came from an era of shorter ADT and different salvage options; whether a metastasis-free gain translates to survival when the control arm already receives two years of ADT plus pelvic RT is precisely what remains open. PCSS sits at 99% in both arms at four years and the OS interval spans 0.49 to 1.59, so the survival question is unanswered rather than negative.

Staging deserves its own caution. Metastases were defined by CT and technetium bone scan. In a population increasingly staged with PSMA PET, some patients classed here as nonmetastatic would be upstaged, and some MFS events would be detected earlier. That likely shifts absolute event rates more than the relative effect, but the 95% versus 88% four-year figures should not be transplanted directly onto PSMA-staged patients.

The toxicity cost appears modest: grade 3 or higher events rose from 36% to 43%, with fatigue the main added cluster and no excess in fractures or cardiac events. For the very high-risk patient already committed to two years of ADT and pelvic RT, the result makes darolutamide a credible intensification partner; what would make it wrong is an OS analysis that fails to follow the surrogate.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The RT backbone was fixed: prostate or prostate bed plus pelvic nodes in both arms, so the HR 0.42 adds to elective nodal RT rather than replacing it. Benefit was reported consistent for salvage RT and for CT node-positive pts (29%), but only 15% had prior RP and subgroup HRs are not in source.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Darolutamide 600 mg BID for 96 wk on top of 96 wk ADT cut MFS-CI events 27 vs 63 with G≥3 AEs 43% vs 36%, and fractures and cardiac G≥2 events no higher than placebo. OS (HR 0.88) and PCSS remain immature, so the ARSI choice in this setting hinges on surrogacy holding.

papers.title: Darolutamide with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) and definitive or salvage locoregional radiation therapy (RT) for localised, very high-risk prostate cancer: Interim analysis of an international, placebo-controlled, randomised phase 3 trial (DASL-HiCaP; ANZUP1801)
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract LBA4 · Presidential Symposium I · 2026-10-24 · presented by Tamim Niazi (Montreal, Canada, QC) · NCT04136353

Background: We evaluated the addition of darolutamide to standard of care ADT and RT for very high-risk localised or biochemically persistent/recurrent prostate cancer within 1 year after radical prostatectomy (RP).
Methods: Participants (pts) were prescribed an LHRH analog for 96 weeks plus RT to prostate/prostate bed and pelvic nodes and randomised 1:1 to darolutamide 600 mg vs placebo, twice daily for 96 weeks. The primary endpoint was metastasis-free survival based on conventional imaging with CT and/or technetium bone scan (MFS-CI, as per ICECaP surrogacy for OS). PSA-progression free survival (PFS), prostate cancer specific survival (PCSS), and overall survival (OS) were secondary endpoints. The protocol specified a single interim analysis after 87 MFS-CI events, with IDSMC review for external disclosure if the 2-sided, stratified log-rank p-value for MFS-CI was <0.012.
Results: We randomised 1,106 pts from 30APR20 to 09AUG23 with median age 71 (IQR 65-75), pelvic nodal involvement on CT in 29%, Gleason score 9-10 in 73%, and prior RP in 15%. Median follow-up was 3.8 years (IQR 3.3 to 4.5). MFS-CI was longer amongst those assigned darolutamide vs placebo: 4-year MFS-CI 95% vs 88%, hazard ratio 0.42 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.66), 27 vs 63 events, p=0.0001. PSA-PFS, PCSS, and OS are shown below. The proportions of pts experiencing grade ≥2 of the following AE clusters of special interest (darolutamide vs placebo) were: fatigue/asthenia (14% vs 10%), hypertension (7% vs 9%), fractures (2% vs 3%), and cardiac (3% vs 3%). Any AE grade ≥3 was experienced by 43% vs 36% of pts, respectively.
Conclusions: Darolutamide significantly improved MFS-CI when added to ADT and loco-regional RT for very high-risk localised, or biochemically persistent/recurrent prostate cancer. Follow-up is ongoing to confirm the surrogacy of MFS-CI for OS. papers.title: Inflammatory and epigenetic signatures in progressive brain metastases after cranial radiotherapy
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 703RO · Rapid oral: CNS tumours · 2026-10-23 · presented by Ariane Steindl (Vienna, Austria)

Background: Given the high rate of early recurrence in brain metastases (BM), factors driving progression remain poorly understood. This study aimed to characterize genetic, epigenetic, and inflammatory signatures in progressive BM after different therapeutic strategies.
Methods: A total of 153 patients undergoing surgical resection for progressive BM were included and stratified according to prior treatment: radiotherapy (n=43), systemic therapy (n=37), radio- and systemic therapy (n=10), or treatment-naive (n=63). Tumor specimens were analyzed with exome-sequencing, DNA methylation profiling, and immunohistochemistry.
Results: Compared with treatment-naive BM, BM resected due to progression to prior radiotherapy demonstrated significantly reduced densities of immune-activating tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) such as CD3+ (median 71 vs. 494 cells/mm2,), CD8+ (44 vs. 187 cells/mm2), and CD45RO+ cells (104 vs. 302 cells/mm2). In contrast, densities of immunosuppressive TILs were increased (FOXP3+: 215 vs. 41cells/mm2). Among treatment-naive patients, 35 developed intracranial relapse and underwent a second resection. Of these, 65.7% did not receive any therapy in between, whereas 34.3% received CNS-radiotherapy between resections. Here, patients who received radiotherapy exhibited modest alterations in DNA methylation compared to those without radiotherapy. These changes were predominantly characterized by hypermethylation in irradiated lesions including pathways associated with immunomodulation, therapy resistance, and interactions with the neural and vascular microenvironment. Comparative genetic profiling did not identify differences in the mutational landscape between progressive lesions, irrespective of prior therapy.
Conclusions: In this study, BM progressing after prior cranial radiotherapy were associated with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, along with modest DNA methylation changes and enrichment of pathways related to immunomodulation and tumor survival. In combination with the clinical observation of varying responses to immunotherapy in progressive BM post-radiotherapy, our data warrant for further investigation for the optimal treatment sequencing in BM patients.

papers.title: Randomized phase II trial investigating addition of trotabresib (CC-90010) to radiotherapy and temozolomide in patients with newly diagnosed IDH wild-type glioblastoma
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 692O · Proffered paper: CNS tumours · 2026-10-25 · presented by Angelo Dipasquale (Rozzano, Italy) · NCT04324840

Background: Patients with IDH wild-type glioblastoma (GBM) invariably experience recurrence despite standard-of-care (SOC) including surgery, radiotherapy, and temozolomide. Bromodomain and extra-terminal proteins (BET) are epigenetic regulators of cell cycle progression overexpressed in GBM. Trotabresib (T) is an oral BET inhibitor that showed brain penetration and tolerable safety profile at a dose of 30 mg/day 4 days on/24 days off in combination with SOC.
Methods: Patients with newly diagnosed IDH wild-type GBM (ndGBM) were randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive T + SOC (arm A) or SOC alone (arm B). The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS), defined as the time from randomization to RANO disease progression by local investigators or death. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the time from randomization to death. Safety profile was assessed with CTCAE V5 and dose reductions/interruptions between arms were compared using odds ratios (ORs).
Results: A total of 184 patients were randomized to arm A (n=124) or arm B (n=60). At the time of database lock, 136 patients experienced a PFS event. At a median follow-up of 15 months, PFS did not favour the experimental arm, with a median PFS (mPFS) of 7.9 vs 8.2 months and 12-month PFS rates of 22.2% vs 38.9% in arms A and B, respectively (p 0.048). No difference in OS was observed (median OS: 16.9 vs 16.7 months in arms A and B, respectively; p 0.898). The most frequent ≥ grade 3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and lymphopenia (37%, 16.8%, and 8.4% in arm A vs 15.3%, 8.5%, and 11.9% in arm B). Dose reductions and interruptions due to TRAEs were significantly more frequent in arm A (43.7% and 49.6%) than in arm B (18.6% and 28.8%), with ORs of 3.39 (95% CI 1.64–7.02; p 0.001) and 2.43 (95% CI 1.25–4.74; p 0.009), respectively.
Conclusions: The addition of trotabresib to SOC did not improve PFS in patients with ndGBM. Dose reductions and interruptions due to TRAEs were more frequent in the experimental arm and may have negatively impacted PFS. These findings suggest that novel drugs in ndGBM should carefully consider tolerability to ensure proper delivery of SOC and maximize clinical benefit. Dr. M. Simonelli and Dr. M. Vieito have contributed equally to this study.
Clinical trial identification: NCT04324840.
